The motif of exile or estrangement (ightirâb here) recalls Suhrawardi's “Western Exile” (al-ghorbat al-gharbîya). Likewise, the motif of Seraphiel's two wings recalls Gabriel's two wings in Risâla-ye âwâz-e parr-e Jabrâ'yel. There is, however, a difference: here Seraphiel is the angel at the summit of all beings, whereas for Suhrawardi Gabriel is the tenth of the hierarchical Intellects, the “Active Intellect” and Holy Spirit, the angel of the human species to whom the story of the White Cloud earlier alluded. ↩

We published a study of the Shaykhi school in Shiite theology as the opening article of the Annuaire de la Section des Sciences religieuses de l'École des Hautes Études, 1960–1961, pp. 1–59. The same text was later reproduced in facsimile with a special introduction and a Persian translation by M. Ferîdûn Bahmanyâr (Maktab-e shaykhî az Hikmat-e ilâhî-e shî'î), Tehran, 1346/1967. The study was prompted by an important book (see p. 214, n. 7, below) by Sarkâr Âghâ, the shaykh of the Shaykhi community, whose work we discuss in the following pages. We believe we interpreted his thought faithfully. When he was able to read our study in Mr Bahmanyâr's careful translation, he gave it his full approval. We recall with sadness the outstanding spiritual personality of this shaykh, whose friendship honored us for many years and from whom we learned so much. He was taken from his disciples and friends only recently, on 3 December 1969. His son Shaykh 'Abdol-Rezâ Khân succeeded him as head of the Shaykhi community. Let this also be an occasion to pay tribute to another distinguished figure in the Shaykhi silsila, or chain of spiritual transmission: Shaykh Ishaq Ebrâhîmî Âghâ-Zâdeh, who died exactly two years earlier (December 1967). For twenty years his friendship opened to us the intricacies of Shaykhi bibliography. Although a number of pages from the original study are reproduced here, the present treatment expands it sufficiently to make it something new. See also our “Pour une morphologie de la spiritualité shî'ite,” Eranos-Jahrbuch XXIX/1960, pp. 71 ff. The French section of our edition and translation of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, Le Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques (Kitâb al-Mashâ'ir) (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. 10), Tehran–Paris, 1964, includes translations of many passages from Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's commentary on that same work. Finally, numerous passages from the works of Shaykhi masters mentioned here have been translated in our Terre céleste et corps de résurrection: de l'Iran mazdéen à l'Iran shî'ite, Paris, 1961. ↩

We have already referred to Majlisî's monumental encyclopedia (d. 1111/1700). The typeset edition under way in Tehran since 1957 is intended to comprise fifty double volumes in quarto. We shall have occasion later to discuss collections assembled by the Shaykhi school. ↩

As for the traditional precursors of the Shaykhi school, future research should note the Shiite figures whom Khwânsârî lists (ibid.) as “links in the chain of transmission,” stretching back to the holy Imams, of akhbâr (traditions) with a particularly “gnostic” character. First are three close companions of the Fifth and Sixth Imams (Mohammad Bâqir, d. 115/733, and Ja'far Sâdiq, d. 148/765): Mofazzal b. 'Omar al-Jo'fî, Jâbir al-Ansârî, and Jâbir al-Jo'fî (the importance of their riwâyât, or transmitted accounts, in Ismaili theosophy is well known). Next is Shadhân ibn al-Khalîl Neyshâpûrî, an associate of the Ninth Imam, Mohammad Jawâd (d. 220/835; Mâmâqânî, Tanqîh al-Maqâl, 5470); Abû Ja'far Moh. Saffâr Qommî (d. 290/903), who knew the Eleventh Imam, Hasan 'Askarî (d. 260/874), and his son, who became the Hidden Imam; Saffâr wrote the Basâ'ir al-darajât (Rayhânat al-adab, II, p. 483, no. 873). Then Farât b. Ibrâhîm al-Kûfî (Mâmâqânî, 9412), one of Ibn Bâbûyeh's sources and author of one of the earliest Shiite tafsîrs (alongside which we may place the tafsîr attributed to the Eleventh Imam); 'Alî b. Ibrâhîm ibn Mâhûyeh Qazwînî (ibid., 8202); Shaykh Sâdûq Ibn Bâbûyeh of Qomm (d. 381/991), one of the foremost Shiite theologians of his generation and author of some three hundred works, particularly the Kitâb al-Majâlis (Rayhânat, II, p. 470, no. 855); Sayyed Razî (d. 406/1015), particularly his Kitâb al-A'imma (ibid., II, p. 259, no. 539); Qotboddîn Sa'îd Râwendî (d. 573/1177–1178), buried in Qomm at the shrine of Hazrat Fâtima, younger sister of the Eighth Imam (ibid., p. 305, no. 477); Yahyâ ibn Batrîq (d. 600/1284, as given in the source), especially his Khasâ'is (a comprehensive work on the First Imam) and 'Omdat (ibid., V, p. 270, no. 532); Sayyed Razîoddîn 'Alî b. Tâ'ûs (d. 664/1265–1266; ibid., VI, p. 60, no. 67); 'Alî ibn 'Isâ Arbelî (d. 696/1296–1297), author of Kashf al-Ghamma (ibid., I, p. 56, no. 121); and finally Mollâ Rajab Borsî (d. ca. 800/1397), best known for Mashâriq al-Anwâr, written around 774/1372. Under Shâh Solaymân, that work received a monumental Persian commentary, Matâli' al-asrâr, by Hasan Khatîb Qârî Mashhadî, comprising 503 folio leaves (see Annuaire de la Section des Sciences religieuses, 1968–1969, pp. 148 ff.). Rajab Borsî is often quoted by Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (ibid., II, p. 259, no. 539). This list is far from complete. It needs to be developed both to write a full history of Shiite theology and to locate the Shaykhi school within it. ↩
See our edition and translation of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, Le Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques (above, p. 206, n. 1), index under “Ahmad Ahsâ'î (Shaykh).” ↩

We mention A. L. M. Nicolas's Essai sur le cheïkhisme, Paris, 1910, only for the record. It is no longer genuinely usable: the entire work rests solely on the polemical account of an opponent of Shaykhism who understood very little of it, and its technical vocabulary is highly unreliable. E. G. Browne gave a short account of Shaykhism in his Traveller's Narrative, II, pp. 243–244. We need not discuss Babism or Bahaism in their own right here, because, as we shall note below, both movements placed themselves ipso facto outside Shiism. When Baha'is express admiration for Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, one can only agree. But when they claim him as their spiritual ancestor, that unwarranted claim must be rejected. There are, we might say, two ways of “leaving” a school. One may flow from it as a stream flows from a spring. Or one may leave it as someone leaves a room, slamming the door—that is, in a way that makes it difficult to claim descent from those who remained inside. ↩

His genealogy runs: Shaykh Ahmad ibn al-Shaykh Zayn al-'Âbidîn ibn al-Shaykh Ibrâhîm ibn al-Saqr ibn Ibrâhîm ibn al-Dâghir. It was with the last-named that the family gave up Bedouin life, settled near al-Ahsâ', and definitively adopted Twelver Shiism (hence Shaykh Ahmad adds after their names the invocation Ghafara Allâh lahom ajma'in: “May God forgive them all”). Consider the episode reported by the author of Tanbîh al-ghâfilîn, from a manuscript in Mîrzâ Ismâ'îl Tabrîzî's own hand. In Basra the shaykh met a man renowned both for his moral character and his learning. He asked him for lessons in hikmat (philosophical wisdom), but the man excused himself because of pressing administrative duties. The shaykh then asked him to name what he regarded as the foundation of a philosophical teaching. He replied: “Do not stop at movements; seek what sets movements in motion. Do not stop at causes; seek what gives causes their causality. Living beings move toward God along the longitudinal (or vertical) dimension; minerals (inert things) move toward God along the latitudinal (or horizontal) dimension.” (Silsilat al-tûl and silsilat al-'arz are characteristic terms of Suhrawardi's “Eastern theosophy.”) “You will then see the mountains you thought immovable begin to move as clouds move” (Quran 27:90). “On hearing these words from this perfected man,” the shaykh added, “many difficulties that had remained in my mind concerning philosophical questions were resolved. I asked him for guidance on the Itinerarium ad Deum, the journey toward God. ‘How, in your view,’ I asked, ‘is it possible to reach God?’ ‘Cast this world far from you,’ he replied. I left his majlis (gathering), and in my heart there remained no trace of love for this world” (p. 183). ↩

For six of these ijâzât, see the list of shaykhs on pp. 188–189 of the same work. They include ijâzât-e rawâyat (licenses certifying the right to transmit texts or traditions) and ijâzât-e dirâyat (licenses attesting the ability to teach and interpret on one's own authority). An ijâzat is a “license” a shaykh gives to a disciple who has studied with him for several years, covering books they have studied together. It is therefore an essentially personal certificate. This gives it its special significance: such licenses authenticate spiritual lines of descent. For this reason we shall take account of the ijâzât of each of the Mashâyekh (Shaykhi masters). ↩

According to his account, his father repented of his takfîr (declaration that another Muslim is an unbeliever) toward the end of his life. Over the centuries, Shiites had filled the Baqî' cemetery with rich and pious monuments—domes, chapels, and shrines. When the Wahhabis established their rule in Arabia after entering Mecca (1924), the entire complex was demolished in the name of religious puritanism and reduced to ruins. During a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1956, the Iranian sovereign, accompanied by his entire entourage, made a lengthy visit to the Baqî' and paused before the sites of the tombs revered by Shiites. Restoration was then promised wherever possible. The event caused a particular stir because an Iranian sovereign had not visited these places for a considerable time; Iranian periodicals published many illustrations of the occasion. ↩

Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ (pp. 263–265), reproducing in full Khwânsârî's remarks about Shaykh Ahmad and his misguided disciples, points out a remarkable mistranslation (of the word âlat). Its original author is probably unknown, but subsequent chroniclers copied it without checking. Where Khwânsârî says of these misguided disciples that “all they did was practice ta'wîl”—that is, give esoteric interpretations of the lessons they heard from Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kâzem—this was translated: “The shaykh's disciples were the organ (instrument, means) of ta'wîl (!).” ↩

Compare this declaration of our author's Imamite faith: “Fully acknowledging Muhammad's prophetic message entails love and devotion to the Imams of his house and to their teaching. If this is Islam and professing Shiism (tashayyo'), so be it. If it is called error or falling short, so be it. If it is called excessive exaltation (gholow), so be it. Let all those who behave as Sunni theologians and refuse to acknowledge the eternal, inalienable preeminence of the holy Imams call us extremists (gholât) if they wish. If extremism means placing the Imams below the rank of divinity but above all creatures, as close to God as possible, we acknowledge that this is, God willing, our only title to glory” (p. 40). These words point directly to the metaphysical level of the doctrine of the Imams. ↩

In Ismaili gnosis the Nâtiq is the prophet sent as the “Speaker” who announces revealed law in its outward, literal form, while the Imam is the “Silent One” (sâmit), who possesses its ta'wîl—the inward meaning of that Revelation. See our Trilogie ismaélienne, index under Nâtiq, and our study “Le « Livre du Glorieux » de Jâbir ibn Hayyân” (Eranos-Jahrbuch XVIII/1950), pp. 66 ff. ↩

Note that imâm, even within Shiism, can also be used in two different senses. Properly speaking—in its true sense—it refers to the “Twelve Most Holy Persons.” We therefore capitalize “Imam” when using it in that sense, to make the difference clear. In the akhbâr, however, the word is sometimes applied metaphorically (majâz) to eminent Shiites. In everyday usage, one speaks of an imam serving a mosque, an imâm-jom'eh (Friday-prayer imam), an “imam of the grammarians,” and so on. These are all metaphorical uses (p. 125). ↩
